_comment: The tenant's policy on the wire, exactly as the backend answers GET /v1/policy (ST-047).
Read by both ends and by neither's production code, like summarize-request.v1.json, but in the other
direction: the backend's TenantPolicyResponse writes this shape and the client's PolicySync reads it
into TenantPolicy. The field names ARE the contract, and here a drift is not a failed request but a
quiet one: a renamed localOnlyLocked would read as false, and an admin-locked local-only setting
would become the technician's to change (INV-11). So the client refuses a policy with a field
missing, or of another type than here, and keeps the last one it synced.
Growing it: a new field may be added here once the backend sends it. The client reads it only as an
optional TenantPolicy parameter with a default, so an older backend that leaves it out still syncs.
A new field the client must refuse to go without belongs in tenant-policy.v2.json, after every
backend sends it; otherwise every policy from an older backend is refused and sync stops.
Every value here differs from the defaults (version "default", 7 days, everything false), so a field
either side stopped reading or writing shows up as a wrong value, not as a coincidence. Nothing here
is content (INV-10): a policy says what the client does, not what it saw.
ST-113 added the four update fields, optional on the client with these defaults: updateChannel
"stable", updateChannelLocked false (the technician chooses), updateCheckHours 24 (0 turns checks
off), updateChecksUnderLocalOnly false (no update checks while local-only is on).
